background.definition: Bell's palsy is an acute, usually temporary, idiopathic paralysis of the facial nerve, typically involving one side of the face.

list.listitem: Incidence is 0.2 people affected per 1000 per year.
Lifetime prevalence is 1/60 people affected.
Peak incidence is in the fourth decade.
There is an 8% risk of recurrence in previously affected individuals.
Unknown; cause may be related to viral exposure, autoimmunity, cold exposure, or structural or solid lesions.
Diabetes and pregnancy are known risk factors.
Vaccination against COVID-19 with mRNA vaccine is associated with a very small absolute risk of Bell's palsy (0.03% vs 0.01%, odds ratio 3.6, 95% CI 1.1-11.7).
Swelling and inflammation of the facial nerve lead to unilateral facial paralysis.
They also lead to lacrimal and salivary gland dysfunction.
Mononuclear cell infiltration is seen histologically.
Diagnosis is largely clinical based on the onset of acute unilateral facial paralysis over 1 to 7 days. C
Specific testing and screening are not usually indicated but can be done in special populations. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Lyme disease, meningitis, osteomyelitis, otitis, Mycobacterium leprae
Look for other evidence of sarcoid
History should give this though keep an index of suspicion
Other distinguishing features may be evident; consider imaging
Initial presentation of Guillain-Barre syndrome is similar to that of Bell's palsy

list.listitem: Complete cranial nerve examination reveals unilateral facial paralysis without any nerve sparing, especially in the forehead. Facial drooping is evident on the affected side with salivary pooling in the affected side of the mouth. Onset of symptoms is typically over 1 to 3 days.
Perform a careful head, ears, eyes, nose, and throat (HEENT) examination. The affected eye cannot close and may paradoxically appear to have increased tearing.
While sensation is preserved, patients may complain of subjective "numbness" as well as decreased taste, phonophobia, ear pain, or loss of corneal reflex.
Note recent cold exposure, viral infection, or presence of other risk factors.
Note any recent rashes, fevers, or arthralgias or history of previous palsy. Also note any history of exposure to new medicines, vaccines, viruses, or other vectors of potential neurologic disease.
Bell's palsy is largely a clinical diagnosis, and diagnostic testing is usually not indicated or needed.
Patients with risk factors can be screened for diabetes mellitus, which can occur in up to 10% of affected individuals.
Lyme titers can be checked if exposure is suspected.

Imaging of the head probably does not affect outcome but can be considered if there is forehead sparing and a mass lesion is suspected or if symptoms do not resolve within 2 weeks. A single study found that diameter of the distal facial (VII) nerve on ultrasound is a good predictor of favorable or unfavorable outcome.
CSF protein and cell counts are mildly elevated in some cases. EMG studies, nerve conduction studies, and blink reflex testing can be considered with persistent symptoms or uncertain diagnosis.
Unilateral facial paralysis is usually diagnostic in and of itself; laboratory evaluation is usually not indicated. Consider fasting glucose if diabetes is suspected.
Duration of longer than 2 weeks or areas of nerve sparing should prompt imaging of the head to rule out mass lesion.
Patients with bilateral palsy and palsy unresponsive to treatment within 2 to 3 weeks should be referred to a neurologist.
Early use (within 3 days of symptom onset) of a 10-day course of corticosteroids increases the likelihood of full recovery (NNT = 6-10). A
Antiviral medications are no longer recommended, based on the most recent publications and a Cochrane review. B
Prevention of corneal complications in the eye is vital. Frequent use of artificial tears is recommended. C

Early use (in the first 3 days) of corticosteroids for 10 days of therapy results in lower rates of incomplete recovery at 6 months or later (22% vs 33%; NNT = 10). This practice is supported by a large recent systematic review that found benefit from corticosteroids but not antivirals; recommended total steroid dose should be at least 450 mg of prednisone or equivalent.

A trial randomized 187 children with Bell's palsy to 1mg/kg/day up to 50 mg of prednisolone for 10 days or placebo. The study found small numeric benefits (NNT = 17 at 6 months) but the study was underpowered and the differences were not statistically significant.

Antiviral use with or without corticosteroids has not been shown to be effective. While two smaller studies showed a slightly higher percentage of full recovery using combination therapy, the largest and best designed study to date showed no benefit to acyclovir (with or without steroids). A Cochrane review showed no benefit based on their review of 14 RCTs with 2488 participants.
The frequent use of artificial tears in the eye on the affected side is strongly recommended to prevent corneal complications. Lid taping and/or eye patching can also be considered.

Surgical therapy is limited. It is generally reserved for cases of total failure to recover and involves techniques of reanastomosing cranial nerves and surgical nerve decompression. A systematic review identified two trials with 65 participants, neither of which identified any benefit between operated and non-operated hands, although the quality and size of the studies was low.
Hearing loss is a potential surgical complication.

Currently available evidence on the efficacy of acupuncture is not of sufficient scientific quality to warrant recommending it for the treatment of Bell's palsy. A 2010 systematic review identified 6 studies with 537 patients, and a 2019 systematic review found 11 studies with 1258 patients, but studies were heterogeneous, of poor quality and did not report key clinical outcomes.

Two small, low-quality trials of tailored facial exercises found that facial exercises may improve facial function in patients with moderate facial paralysis and prevent sequelae in acute cases. There is insuffficient evidence to determine if other physical therapy modalities such as electrical stimulation are effective at reducing symptoms.
There is insufficient evidence that hyperbaric oxygen therapy improves recovery of facial function in adults with moderate to severe Bell's palsy.
The most common complication is protracted or partial loss of facial nerve function, with abnormal tearing, muscle weakness, and muscle spasm. Surgical management may be considered in severe cases.
Inability to close the eye on the affected side can lead to corneal ulcerations and/or abrasions from drying and exposure. Artificial tears and eye protection are recommended.
Complications of steroid and antiviral use are rare, given the short duration of therapy.
Expect complete or nearly complete recovery in 85% or more of cases. A
Outpatient follow-up is important for severe or slowly resolving cases. C
Recovery of function and prevention of complications is the main treatment goal. C
Within 3 weeks, 85% of patients or more recover spontaneously.
Of these, 71% recover full function.
Final recovery may take 4 to 8 weeks or more to attain.
Complete or partial recovery is expected.
Cases of no recovery at all are rarely seen.
No specific follow-up testing is indicated.
Follow as outpatient in severe or unresolving cases (q 1-3 weeks, as needed).
Monitor for corneal or tearing complications.
Consider monthly long-term follow-up or referral in severe cases.
Early access to a health care provider is recommended.
Prevention of complications is important.
Recovery of lost function is the goal and does occur in most cases, regardless of treatment.
Bell's palsy is three times more common in pregnancy than in the nonpregnant state. Symptoms are frequently more severe and recovery rates are lower.
The use of corticosteroids (category C) for Bell's palsy has not been well studied in pregnancy, so their use is controversial. It is effective in non-pregnant patients.
Acyclovir, valacyclovir, and famciclovir (category B) are not beneficial in pregnant or non-pregnant patients are not recommended.
